cards.title: Understanding Semantic Versioning (SemVer)
cards.content:
Modern software development, including Java libraries, relies heavily on Semantic Versioning (SemVer). A version number is formatted as MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH:

  • MAJOR: Incremented for incompatible API changes.
  • MINOR: Incremented for adding backward-compatible functionality.
  • PATCH: Incremented for backward-compatible bug fixes.
// Example: Upgrading from 1.2.3 to 2.0.0 introduces breaking changes!
// Upgrading from 1.2.3 to 1.3.0 is safe and adds new features.

cards.title: Evolution of Java Versioning
cards.content:
Java's versioning format underwent a massive shift over time:

  • Pre-Java 9: Versions were formatted as 1.x (e.g., Java 8 was technically 1.8.0).
  • Java 9 to 21+: A simplified scheme was adopted focusing on the system format: $FEATURE.$INTERIM.$UPDATE.$PATCH.

This means Java 11 is represented simply as version 11, not 1.11.

cards.title: Java's Modern Release Cadence
cards.content:
Since Java 9, Oracle and the OpenJDK community shifted to a predictable six-month release cadence (March and September of every year).

To support enterprise users, certain releases are designated as Long-Term Support (LTS) releases, receiving updates and security patches for years, whereas non-LTS releases are supported for only six months.

cards.title: Detecting Java Version Programmatically
cards.content:
In modern Java (Java 9+), you can easily query the runtime version details using the Runtime.Version class instead of parsing complex property strings manually.

Runtime.Version version = Runtime.version();
int major = version.feature(); // Returns the major feature version (e.g., 17 or 21)
System.out.println("Running on Java Major: " + major);

cards.title: Dependency Versioning in Build Tools
cards.content:
When defining external libraries in Maven (pom.xml) or Gradle (build.gradle), precise version control prevents runtime errors:

  • Strict Versioning: Pinning exact coordinates (e.g., <version>2.4.0</version>).
  • SNAPSHOT Versions: Denoting ongoing development (e.g., 1.0.0-SNAPSHOT). Build tools always check for updates to SNAPSHOT dependencies on remote repositories.

cards.title: Best Practices for Upgrading Java Versions
cards.content:
When upgrading your project's Java Version:

  1. Update Tooling: Ensure IDEs, build plugins (like maven-compiler-plugin), and CI/CD agents support the targeted JDK version.
  2. Verify Transitive Dependencies: Make sure third-party bytecode-manipulation tools (like ASM, ByteBuddy, or Lombok) are upgraded to support target runtime class file versions.
